rv.q: Deep in Irony Spirals, Slam Frank Struggles to Show Its Core
It should unsettle you and entertain you in the same breath, and make you think while you're still laughing.
As far as Hamilton knockoffs go—and there are a lot these days—Fox has actually written one of the better ones, with clever lyrics and catchy tunes.
Sam Lafrage’s direction can’t obscure some of the show’s early book problems.
There are some genuine moments of brilliance, such as Edith’s slam poem, “Yeast of Edith.”
Messrs. Fox and Sinensky, in contrast, press buttons to provoke and please modern audiences without really saying or doing anything original.

But while barreling forward through nearly two hours of song-and-dance-and-derision without let-up (or intermission), the show feels less and less entertaining, and the point of it all seems more and more uncertain.
The jaw-dropping absurdity will continue to tickle your funny bone at the same time you tilt your head, asking yourself, WTF?!
Such work is rare and hard and should be saluted (just not Nazi-style, please).
It's blisteringly funny and offers food for thought some might find hard to digest.
Slam Frank takes aim at every ideology in sight, and its willingness to offend everyone equally makes it the most daring ticket Off-Broadway this fall.
During the 110 minutes of “Slam Frank”, you will be anything but bored.

“Slam Frank” mostly succeeds in satirizing the state of the mainstream American theater, which is inexplicably hell-bent on reimagining decades-old shows written by and for white people with BIPOC casts rather than supporting new work written by artists of diverse backgrounds.

Like many satires, ‘Slam Frank’ is too long, its punchlines too scattershot to sustain a nearly two-hour show Your response ultimately comes down to taste. Too often, ‘Slam Frank’ leaves a bitter one.
The way Slam Frank chooses to address it is quite possibly the most shocking thing I've ever seen in a New York theater.
Linda Purl’s performance makes it unforgettable.

But any musical that opens with multiple projections of Patti LuPone for no apparent reason is out for easy laughs, and its program advisory, “Content Warning: Everything,” conveys what an exhausting experience this is.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this audacious satire that lampoons woke theater culture through an Anne Frank reimagining. Many praise its subversive courage and talented cast, while others find it a muddled, taste-testing provocation that offends indiscriminately.

vr.q: The show is funny. The show is subversive. The show is one of a kind and I think that is the reason to go see this.
